paragraphs.source_en: Perhaps to Americans it is truly regarded as a kind of athletic sport; but even if it is a sport, since it possesses enough power to alarm the whole neighborhood, it can quite well serve as artillery fire, depending on how it is used. Judging from what I have observed with my own eyes, I can only conclude that they are attempting to use this athletic method to achieve the effect of cannon fire. Things, after all, can be made to change this way or that according to how one names them. Since there are people who commit fraud under the name of charity, and people who call their feverish excitement “inspiration” and take pleasure in it, it is hardly impossible that someone should wish to wage war under the name of a baseball game. The explanation given by certain people must refer to baseball as it is generally known in society; the baseball I am now describing is limited to baseball in this special situation, namely siege artillery warfare. I shall now introduce the method of firing dum-dum bullets. In the battery arranged in a straight line, one man grips a dum-dum bullet in his right hand and throws it at the man holding the laundry-pounding club. What this dum-dum bullet is made of, an outsider cannot know; it is something hard and round, like a stone dumpling, carefully wrapped in leather and then sewn together. As I have already explained, once this shell leaves the gunner’s hand and flies forward cutting through the wind, the man standing opposite at once swings up the laundry-pounding club and strikes it back with all his might. Now and then he misses, and the shell goes flying off. Usually, however, there is a tremendous crack, and the shell rebounds. Its force is so great that it could burst the head of my master, afflicted as he is with nervous indigestion. With that alone, the gunners have fulfilled their task. But all around and nearby, hecklers doubling as reinforcements cling about the gunners like swarms of cloud and mist. The instant the club hits the ball, they howl, clap loudly, and shout, “Good, good!” Or they say, “Didn’t that hit him?” Some say, “That ought to work this time.” Others say, “Let’s see whether you’ll behave yourself now!” “Will you surrender or not?” If that were all, it would still be tolerable; but of the shells struck back, one in every three is sure to roll into the grounds of Woryukutsu, for unless the shell rolls in there, the purpose of the attack cannot be achieved. Recently these dum-dum bullets have been manufactured in many places, but they are still quite expensive. Even in war, the gunners cannot obtain an unlimited supply of shells; generally a squad of gunners is allotted only one or two, and they cannot consume one shell every time they fire. So they have established a special squad called the “shell collectors,” who retrieve the shells. If the shell lands in a good place, naturally retrieving it is no trouble; but if it flies into the grass or into someone’s yard, it is not so easily recovered. Therefore, in ordinary times, to save labor they would try as much as possible to knock the “shells” into places where they are easy to retrieve; but the present situation is exactly the opposite. The purpose is no longer play; it lies in war.

paragraphs.source_en: And so they deliberately knock the shells into my master’s yard. Since the shells have fallen in the yard, naturally they must come into the yard to pick them up. The simplest way to enter the yard is to jump over the lattice fence. If they make a commotion inside the fence, my master must get angry; otherwise he has no choice but to lay down his arms and surrender. And once my master gets angry, his head is bound to grow balder and balder.
